A amiga discreta dos três animais desta quadra. 01 · ORIGEM Nascer da lei, não da rua uma polícia desenhada para o processo, não para a cidade A história da Polícia Judiciária começa antes do seu nome. Em 1867, a grande reforma judiciária portuguesa organiza uma polícia civil sob controlo das autoridades judiciais, com atributos de investigação penal — a matriz de tudo o que a PJ viria a ser. Ao contrário da Guarda Nacional Republicana, que nasce militar e cobre o território, esta polícia nasce administrativa e processual: existe para servir o inquérito, não para patrulhar. Essa diferença de berço explica a diferença de carácter que ainda hoje separa as duas instituições: o tigre dessa outra história é visível na rua da cidade; a serpente só se mostra quando o processo a chama. 1867 A reforma judiciária cria a polícia civil Sob direcção das autoridades judiciais nasce numa reorganização da justiça uma polícia de investigação penal com quadros civis — o embrião institucional da futura PJ, concentrada em Lisboa e Porto. 1936 A sombra política ganha corpo próprio O Estado Novo cria a PVDE, depois PIDE, separando a vigilância política da investigação comum. A polícia civil continua a investigar o crime — mas vive na sombra projetada pela máquina política que a cercava. 1944 A cisão: PSP e PJ dividem a polícia civil Uma reorganização legislativa divide a polícia civil em duas: a polícia de segurança (PSP) fica com a presença urbana; a polícia judiciária fica com a investigação do crime, colocada sob a tutela do Ministro da Justiça. É aqui que a serpente nasce como instituição distinta — desenhada para o processo, não para a rua. 1976 A refundação democrática Depois do 25 de Abril, uma lei orgânica devolve-lhe um desenho civil e democrático: coadjuvar as autoridades judiciais na investigação, com subordinação ao Ministro da Justiça. O dragão e o tigre ficaram na Administração Interna; a serpente ficou junto dos tribunais. 1993 A lei orgânica que ainda define a PJ O decreto-lei orgânico de 1993 fixa o desenho actual: órgão de polícia criminal, serviço central do Estado, dirigido operacionalmente na investigação pelo Ministério Público e dependente do Ministério da Justiça — com poder de coordenação sobre restantes órgãos de polícia criminal na perseguição criminal grave. 2007 → hoje Era digital e regras comuns A lei orgânica da criminalidade em matéria de segurança acerca o uso da força para todas as polícias; a PJ ganha unidades dedicadas ao cibercrime e à criminalidade tecnológica quando o crime emigra para as redes. A serpente muda de pele — a natureza, não. Um dossiê honesto não esconde a memória do Estado Novo: a investigação criminal portuguesa cresceu dentro de um regime autoritário, e a proximidade com o poder político da época é parte da herança. É a mesma linha ética que este blog já traçou a propósito da GNR: uma instituição é uma estrutura, não uma ideologia — e é precisamente porque é estrutura que sobrevive às revoluções e herda, das duas maneiras, o que os regimes lhe pediram: GNR — O Dragão que Guarda a Lei . 02 · SÍMBOLOS A serpente e o Macaco uma leitura, não um brasão Comecemos pela honestidade: a serpente não aparece oficialmente no emblema da Polícia Judiciária. É a leitura deste blog — e talvez por isso a leitura mais fiel. Brasões oficiais são administrados por despachos; as serpentes são atribuídas pela prática. E o que a prática mostra é um animal que não ruge: escuta, aguarda, avalia distâncias, e só então morde. Quem já acompanhou um inquérito longo reconhece o movimento — o silêncio calibrado, a vantagem do tempo, a precisão do gesto final. Nas culturas onde este blog bebe os seus símbolos, a serpente é ambígua por natureza. É veneno e é remédio; é o longo casulo de Asclépio que ainda hoje assinala a medicina; é o ouroboros que devora a própria cauda e fala de ciclos; na Ásia, a cobra-naga protege templos e guardiões, e o dragão de Dehua é precisamente a mesma criatura sublimina, elevada a celestial. A serpente muda de pele sem mudar de natureza — a metáfora perfeita para uma instituição que reformou nomes, diplomas e métodos desde 1867 sem nunca abandonar a função de investigar o que os outros escondem. E o Macaco? O Macaco é a pessoa curiosa que olha para tudo e publica tudo — o oposto comportamental da serpente. A amizade secreta entre ambos funciona assim: a serpente vê o que o Macaco não consegue ver, porque desliza por dentro; o Macaco conta o que a serpente não pode contar, porque assina o silêncio. Um guarda o segredo; o outro documenta a sua existência. É uma amizade de funções, não de métodos — e, como todas as amizades de trabalho, depende que cada uma respeite o território da outra: o Macaco não deve morder, a serpente não deve publicar. Comentário pedagógico — ler símbolos sem os transformar em propaganda Um símbolo atribuído por leitura — não por despacho — obriga a mais cuidado, não a menos: ninguém nos autorizou a dizer que a PJ é uma serpente, e por isso o teste é o comportamento observável, não o emblema. Quando o blog atribui animais às instituições, lê comportamentos de longo-prazo; o mesmo fez com o Macaco e as culturas asiáticas e com o discurso que fundou esta abordagem. Para aprofundar essa leitura: Discurso do Eterno Macaco às Forças de Segurança do Mundo , What Monkeys Symbolize on Asian Cultures? e The Wise who Refuse to Participate on ... — os três sábios que veem, ouvem e calam, a disciplina original da serpente. 03 · MANDATO O mandato de uma polícia do juiz depois do crime, antes do tribunal O desenho institucional da PJ é singular em Portugal. As outras forças de segurança dependem do Ministério da Administração Interna; a PJ depende do Ministério da Justiça. As restantes patrulham; a PJ investiga. As restantes respondem a ocorrências; a PJ responde a processos. Na arquitectura do Estado, é a única polícia concebida para trabalhar dentro do inquérito criminal — e é por isso que a direcção da investigação cabe ao Ministério Público, e ao juiz de instrução cabe autorizar os actos que a lei lhe reserva. Esse desenho tem consequências práticas que valem a pena listar: Prioridade por gravidade, não por geografia. A PJ não tem territorialidade própria; trabalha onde o processo exigir. É chamada quando o caso excede a dimensão que as polícias territoriais tratam. Coadjuvação e coordenação. Nos crimes de maior gravidade e na criminalidade organizada, cabe-lhe coordenar os restantes órgãos de polícia criminal na actividade processual — um papel de rede, não de território. Perícia própria. O laboratório científico da PJ é uma instituição dentro da instituição: biologia forense, balística, informática forense, entidades que fazem do laudo pericial o produto mais duradouro da PJ. Internacional. Criminalidade organizada não respeita fronteiras; a PJ vive de intercâmbio com parceiros europeus e internacionais — de Europol a INTERPOL — e de ordens europeias de detenção e redes judiciárias. Sigilo como instrumental de trabalho. Diferentemente das polícias de presença, grande parte do trabalho da PJ decorre sob sigilo legalmente condicionado — garantindo defesa da investigação, mas também criando as tensões que este dossiê vai endereçar nas sombras. Numa frase A PSP é a ferocidade visível da cidade e a GNR é a guarda do território; a PJ é o silêncio técnico que atravessa o processo — a serpente entre os dois animais de farda, com o juiz por garante e o Ministério Público por timoneiro. Comentário pedagógico — por que a diferença de tutela importa Ter uma polícia de investigação fora da Administração Interna é uma decisão de desenho do Estado: aproxima a investigação do tribunal e afasta-a do risco de instrumentalização pelo governo de turno. Não é garantia absoluta de independência — veremos nas sombras — mas é um travão estrutural que merece ser lido como tal. Quem quiser comparar lógicas de organização policial tem no arquivo um manual técnico e uma leitura do que acontece quando o pensamento se delega à farda: Police Groups in Society — A Technical Manual e A Polícia não Pensa . 04 · ESTRUTURA O mapa das divisões atuais A PJ organiza-se em direcções centrais e unidades especializadas, complementadas por delegações regionais. Este quadro é uma janela de leitura pública — os nomes exactos e as siglas vigentes confirmam-se sempre na fonte oficial, porque as siglas dos diplomas mudam mais depressa do que os blogues. A lógica, essa, é estável: um departamento por família de criminalidade grave, um laboratório para a prova, unidades técnicas para o digital, e uma rede territorial de delegações que dá aos tribunais de todo o país um ponto de contacto. Validate Level 1 Chapter 1 LEVEL 1 What a “police group” is — and is not In technical terms, a police group is a bounded organization with authority to apply coercive force under a legal framework, a defined jurisdiction, internal hierarchy, and accountability channels. The group may be called police, gendarmerie, constabulary, civil guard, or something else — the name is local, not universal. Core concepts Jurisdiction — the territory and subject-matter a group is empowered to act in. Hierarchy — the chain of command and rank structure. Function — what the group actually does: patrol, investigate, respond, detain, prevent. Consent / legitimacy — whether the public accepts the group’s right to act. Oversight — independent bodies that inspect, investigate, and discipline. Co-production — the extent to which policing relies on non-police actors (medics, social workers, community members). Concept map Four axes of comparison Every police group can be described along: (1) centralization , (2) armed vs. unarmed routine posture , (3) training depth , (4) oversight independence . These four axes explain most cross-country differences without reducing a country to a stereotype. Watch-out The “best police” trap No single system is universally “best.” Each trades off cost, speed, local knowledge, coercion, and accountability. A system that excels at corruption control may be criticized elsewhere for severity; a decentralized system may be flexible but uneven. Compare dimensions , not medals. Manual convention: when this text labels a decision a “bad decision,” it means a decision that fails its own stated objective and is structurally comparable to similar failures in other systems — it does not claim any country is uniquely bad. Equal weight across systems. Chapter 2 LEVEL 2 How police groups produce their activity Activity is not random. A group’s output — patrols, arrests, reports, stops, prevention — flows from four inputs and one feedback loop. Inputs What feeds the machine Budget & staffing set capacity. Legal mandate sets what is allowed. Data & intelligence set where attention goes. Training & doctrine set the style of action. Change any input and activity changes. Cycle The feedback loop Activity produces records (calls, crimes, stops). Records feed analysis. Analysis changes deployment. Deployment changes activity. The loop is where strategy becomes reality — or where it silently degrades. UK 999/101 calls; US 911 dispatch; Japan koban local reports. 2 · Patrol & visibility Presence meant to deter and to gather local knowledge. Neighborhood beats; koban boxes; foot patrols; random vehicle stops (varies by country). 3 · Investigation Follow-up after an event, including forensics and interviews. Detective branches; specialized units; cross-border cooperation. 4 · Proactive / prevention Acting before harm using patterns, partnerships, and problem-solving. Community policing; intelligence-led deployment; problem-oriented projects (SARA). 5 · Strategic governance Policy, standards, training, oversight, funding choices. National standards bodies; independent complaints offices; academies; budget cycles. Animated cycle: calls → deployment → records → analysis → new deployment. Each society tilts the stack differently. The SARA loop — problem-oriented policing One widely used framework is SARA : S canning, A nalysis, R esponse, A ssessment. It is a decision model that keeps a team from acting on hunches alone. Scanning Spot the recurring problem What keeps happening? Which locations, times, victims, and repeat events form a pattern worth a project — not just one-off calls. Analysis Understand causes Look at the “problem triangle” — likely offender, suitable target, absence of capable guardian — plus environment and incentives. Response Design an intervention Not necessarily “more arrests.” Could be environmental change, partnership with housing/health, targeted deterrence, or removing a contributing condition. Assessment Did it work? Measure before/after on the problem you defined. If it didn’t help, revise. The loop is the point — not the single action. Each system is a bundle of choices. United Kingdom — England & Wales Policing by consent, unarmed routine, regional forces Most officers do not carry firearms and historically rely on public approval. Policing is delivered by regional forces under national training/standards expectations; oversight is via the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC), which handles the most serious matters and sets complaint-handling standards. Good fit: legitimacy-driven, de-escalation culture, independent oversight. Trade-off: capacity strain, uneven local performance, firearm incidents require specially armed units. Japan Koban community policing, long training, high visibility Japan operates roughly 6,000 neighborhood police boxes (koban) staffed around the clock, embedding officers in daily community life — addressing lost-and-found, directions, minor disputes, and local crime prevention alongside law enforcement. Training and academy structure are comparatively long and formal. Good fit: local knowledge, prevention, low threshold for contact. Trade-off: historical debate about closeness of police-community ties and conformity pressure; success partly reflects broader social context. United States Many agencies, decentralized, armed, broad mandate The US has on the order of 18,000 law-enforcement agencies across local, state, and federal levels. Training length is comparatively short on average, and academies historically emphasize technical/firearm skills more than de-escalation and crisis intervention. France Dual national forces plus municipal police France has a dual structure: a National Police (Police nationale) for urban areas and a National Gendarmerie (Gendarmerie nationale) with a rural/military heritage, plus municipal police at the local level. Good fit: federal flexibility, restraint-minded training posture, specialized federal units. Trade-off: coordination across Länder, varied local capacity. It developed a Neighbourhood Police Centre (NPC) model for local one-stop presence, pairs policing with broader corruption-control institutions and policy choices (pay, conditions, enforcement). Below are techniques used (with variation) across societies, followed by the real example of a “bad decision” class and how to avoid it. Improvement levers Lever What it changes Real-world flavour Longer, deeper training Decision quality under stress; de-escalation; legal/ethical judgment. Several European systems train recruits for years and pair academy study with practice; some include degree-level study. Problem-oriented projects (SARA) Shifts from “more of the same” to tailored interventions. Local teams targeting a recurring hotspot or repeat harm with analysis and follow-up assessment. Intelligence-led deployment Prioritization informed by analysis, not only the loudest call. Data-informed resource targeting, with safeguards against bias and over-policing. Co-production / alternative responders Reduces armed escalation by sending the right responder. Unarmed crisis responders for mental-health calls; community support officers handling low-level matters; CAHOOTS-style programs. Independent oversight Improves accountability and public confidence. Watchdog bodies that investigate serious matters and set complaint standards; external audit of use-of-force. Transparency & data Makes activity visible and debatable. Published stop/arrest/use-of-force data; regular public reporting; open methodology. Corruption-control design Reduces rent-seeking and abuse. Pay/conditions, clear anti-corruption institutions, enforcement, and prevention — an integrated approach rather than one silver bullet. Real example: a bad-decision class and why it is equal across systems Consider “escalate-by-default in low-risk encounters.” If routine encounters are handled by maximizing coercion rather than de-escalation, several things happen at once: public trust falls, the encounter set expands (more people are pulled into conflict), and the group spends capacity on avoidable conflict instead of prevention. This is a decision class , not a country trophy. Similar failures can arise wherever doctrine, training, incentives, or data practices push officers toward escalation, silence, or secrecy. The manual treats the quality of the failure as comparable across systems and asks: what input produced it, and which lever would change it? Animated “improvement flywheel”: better training → better decisions → less avoidable conflict → more capacity for prevention → more trust. Step 3 Identify training length/emphasis and doctrine. Step 4 Identify oversight and accountability channels. Step 5 Identify where co-production and alternative responders sit. Step 6 Read the feedback loop: what data is collected, who sees it, and how it changes deployment. policeViolence: Told by a guy who has been on both sides of the shield — and has the bruises and the coffee stains to prove it Don't Hit Grandma With A Sign: How We Stop Police Violence Against Peaceful Manifestations A story in 12 chapters. Funny where it hurts, serious where it counts. If you are a protester, a cop, a mayor, or just someone who pays taxes for helmets to be banged against placards — this is for you. 1. The Square Where Nothing Dangerous Happened (Until The Vans Arrived) Let me tell you how it started, because I was there, with bad shoes and a borrowed sign. Tuesday, 6pm, Republic Square. Or Liberty Square. Honestly every city has the same square — pigeons, a closed kiosk, a statue of a guy on a horse who nobody can name. There were maybe 300 of us. Nurses asking for overtime pay. A couple teachers. Students with too much eyeliner and too little sleep. Dona Lurdes with her cookies. A kid with a drum who could not keep rhythm to save his life. Signs like “WE CAN’T BREATHE ON THESE WAGES” and “MY GRANDMA MARCHES FASTER THAN REFORM.” Dangerous stuff. Extremely dangerous cardboard. We chanted. Badly. Someone started “The people united” and half forgot the words and mumbled. A dog slept through it. A street vendor sold water at double price — capitalism survived the protest just fine. Then you heard them. Not chanting. Engines. Three vans, doors sliding like in movies. Shields, helmets, boots that cost more than my month’s rent. They lined up like we were an invading army. I swear the pigeons were more threatening that day — one actually stole a cop’s sandwich later, true story. Nothing had been broken. Nothing thrown. The only thing in the air was sweat and cheap sunscreen. But the line advanced. And that’s the first lesson I want tattooed on every city hall wall: peace does not break by itself. Someone has to come break it. I’m not an AI writing from a cloud. I’m a man who carried his neighbor’s kid on his shoulders that day because the kid wanted to see. I remember the smell of popcorn from the corner. I remember thinking: if anyone hits anyone here, it won’t be us starting it. We didn’t even have sticks for the signs — they were taped to cardboard tubes so we wouldn’t poke anyone’s eye out. That’s how hardcore we were. 2. Meet Officer Robocop Brain-Optional and His Magic Baton Okay, I’m going to make fun now. Forgive me, but some of it you earn. Every deployment has a Robocop Brain-Optional. You know him. Visor down even though it’s 34 degrees. Chest out. Baton twirling like he’s in a Michael Bay film. He didn’t join to protect. He joined because he liked the uniform in the mirror and because his cousin said you get respect without having to earn it. Field guide to Brain-Optional (subspecies: Escudus erectus ): Identified by shouting “MOVE BACK!” at people who are sitting. Believes a grandma with a Tupperware is a logistical threat. Thinks cameras are weapons. Thinks thinking is disobedience. His baton is magic: one tap turns a nurse into a “rioter,” a student into a “threat,” and his own paycheck into a lawsuit the city will pay, not him. That Tuesday, Brain-Optional found his nemesis: Dona Lurdes. She offered him a cookie. I saw it. “Son, you look hot, eat.” He shouted “DO NOT APPROACH!” She’s 68, 1.58m, approach speed: glacier. He pushed her sign. The sign said “COOKIES FOR FAIR WAGES.” Extremely subversive pastry. Here’s the provocative part, and I mean it: if your threat assessment flags cookies, you are not in security. You are in comedy. And it’s expensive comedy. One shove, one old lady on the ground, ten phones filming, and boom — you just turned 300 peaceful nobodies into 30,000 angry somebodies by tomorrow. Congratulations, genius. You created the danger you were sent to prevent. I’m not saying all cops are like this. I’m saying the ones who are, are loud, hit first, and hide behind the good ones when the video goes viral. And commanders love them until the lawsuit, then they’ve “never seen this officer before in their lives.” 3. Anatomy of Stupidity: Why Beating Peaceful People Is Tactically Idiotic Let me put my teacher hat on, because this story has to teach something useful or it’s just bar talk. Beating a peaceful manifestation is stupid on five levels. Write them down: 1. It doesn’t work. You don’t disperse ideas with bruises. You water them. Every textbook on crowd psychology — and every grandma — knows this. Hit a sitting kid and his entire school shows up next day. Gas a square and you get three squares. 2. It’s expensive. Overtime, medical bills, broken shields, lawsuits, burnt vans next week when people actually get mad. The city pays. That means you pay, even if you cheered for the beating on TV. The baton always bills the taxpayer. 3. It blinds you. Once you start hitting, you can’t tell who is actually dangerous. The one guy who did bring a Molotov hides behind the chaos you created. Good policing is like good surgery: don’t cut everything because one tooth is rotten. 4. It corrupts rookies. The 22-year-old who joined to help finds himself ordered to shove a teacher. He either obeys and hates himself, or disobeys and gets punished. You just taught him law is about obedience, not justice. Ten years later he’s Brain-Optional 2.0. 5. It’s cowardly math. 20 armored cops vs. one kid with a drum is not bravery. Real bravery is standing between traffic and marchers so nobody gets run over. Real bravery is telling your lieutenant “sir, these people are sitting, there’s no lawful reason to charge.” Kid with drum to cop line: “Why are you in armor? We’re not even in tune.” Cop (honest one, whispering): “Tell me about it. I told them we needed water, not shields.” Peaceful crowds are not dangerous. They are inconvenient. They block traffic. They chant off-key. They make politicians uncomfortable. Inconvenience is not danger. If your training confuses the two, your training is the danger. 4. Meet Dona Lurdes, 68, Terrorist Threat Level: Cookies Dona Lurdes is real. I changed her name a little because she’d kill me if I put her address, but everything else is true. Retired cook, widow, knees bad, voice loud. She brings cookies to every march because “people with low sugar make bad decisions — including police.” When Brain-Optional pushed her, she did not throw a brick. She sat down harder. Gravity as resistance. Then she said the most dangerous sentence of the day: “Son, I pay your salary, and I’m disappointed.” Ten phones caught it. That line did more damage to violent policing than any barricade. Humor is a weapon here, and I mean it as tactic: peaceful ridicule exposes stupidity without giving excuse for beating. When cops in armor face grandmas with cookies, who looks strong? Not the armor. My advice to every march: bring grandmas to the front. Not as shields — as mirrors. No officer wants to explain to his own mother why he pepper-sprayed someone’s mother over cardboard. Dona Lurdes later filed a complaint. With receipt for cookies. “Item: 40 cookies, wasted due to shove.” The clerk laughed, then stamped it. Paper is slow, but paper remembers when bruises fade. Keep receipts. Literally. 5. The Other Cop: Mario, Who Reads Orders Twice Now the other side, because I promised, and because it’s true. Mario is 41, two kids, belly from station coffee, 17 years on the force. He was in that line too. Helmet under arm because “if I can’t see faces, I can’t do my job.” When lieutenant shouted “Push them back to the avenue,” Mario did something revolutionary: he looked. He saw kids sitting. Signs. Cookies on pavement. No bricks, no bottles, no knives. He leaned to the rookie next to him: “What exactly are we pushing? Air?” Then he did the four-word magic: walked to lieutenant and said, “Is that lawful, sir?” I didn’t hear it — a journalist friend told me later, and Mario confirmed over beer (he paid, good man). The lieutenant blinked. “It’s an order.” Mario: “Orders need legal basis, sir. What’s the infraction? Assembly is constitutional. No violence, no blockade of emergency route — we can reroute traffic in ten minutes. If we charge, we create the crime.” That pause saved the day from becoming a hospital night. The lieutenant, to his credit, hesitated. Hesitation is underrated. He radioed: “Hold line. No advance unless attacked.” Brain-Optional sulked. Mario handed Dona Lurdes back her Tupperware. Listen: police are useful — essential, even — but only when they question orders. A cop who obeys blindly is just a baton with legs. A cop who thinks is a citizen with authority. The first serves whoever shouts loudest. The second serves law. Lesson from Mario for every cop reading this (and I know some are): Your oath is to the constitution, not to the lieutenant’s mood. “I was following orders” stopped working as an excuse in 1945. If an order tells you to beat peaceful people, that order is unlawful. Refusing it is not disobedience — it’s obedience to higher law. And yes, it takes guts. So does getting hit with a brick, and you signed up for guts. 6. Useful Police 101: What Cops Are Actually For (Hint: Not Piñata Duty) Let’s be provocative but fair: we need police. I need them. You need them. The street vendor needs them when someone actually robs him. The march needs them when a drunk driver tries to plow through. My daughter needs them when she walks home at night. But useful police at a peaceful manifestation do four boring, beautiful things: 1. Protect the march from traffic and from provocateurs. Stand on the edges, backs to protesters, eyes outward. The best cop at a demo is the one you barely notice because he’s stopping cars, not swinging. 2. Talk. “Hey, organizers, where are you heading? Let’s keep one lane open for ambulances, deal?” Ten minutes of talk saves ten hours of ER. Mario does this. Brain-Optional thinks talking is weakness. Talking is tactics. 3. Target only real violence, precisely. If one idiot throws a bottle, you pull that idiot — with minimum force, on camera — not gas the 299 others. Collective punishment is for bad parents, not professionals. 4. Document for truth. Bodycams on. Not off when it gets interesting. A good cop wants footage because footage proves he was good. I once saw Mario carry that kid-with-drum’s drum over a puddle so it wouldn’t get wet. The crowd laughed, clapped. Next chant was “MARIO! MARIO!” He blushed under his cap. That’s authority. Not fear — trust. Fear needs armor. Trust just needs consistency. So yeah, mock the stupid, but recruit the useful. When you chant “cops are...” — finish it with “welcome if they protect.” It confuses Brain-Optional and delights Mario. Provocation with precision. 7. The Order: “Disperse Them” — And The Four Words That Save Lives Every abuse starts with vague words on a radio. “Disperse.” “Clear.” “Restore order.” Order of what? There was order — sitting order, singing order. Here’s what I teach in workshops now (yes, I do them in community halls with bad coffee, come): For cops: the 30-second legality check. 1. What law is being broken, specifically? (Noise after 10pm is not “riot.” Sitting is not “attack.”) 2. Is my action proportionate and necessary? (Baton vs. cardboard = no. Shield wall vs. sitting = no.) 3. Did I warn clearly, give time and exit path? (“Disperse in 2 minutes via north street, water station there” — not a scream while charging.) 4. Would I do this if my mother and my chief were both filming? (They are. Phones everywhere.) If any answer is no — hold, ask, document refusal of unlawful order. Write it. Paper protects thinkers. Mario told me his trick: he repeats the order back loudly. “Sir, confirm: you want us to use force against seated, non-violent people with no emergency blockade?” Nine times out of ten, the commander rephrases to something lawful, because now it’s on record. Bureaucracy, used for good. Beautiful. And commanders: if you give an order you wouldn’t sign with your name in the newspaper tomorrow, don’t give it. “Just clear them, I don’t care how” means “I want violence without responsibility.” Courts translate that now. So do mothers. 8. What Protesters Can Do So Even Dumb Policing Fails Story time again, because preaching bores even me. After the cookie incident, we got smart. Not paranoid — organized. Old Man Joaquim, ex-army, became our “Mario on our side.” He taught: Know the line. March permit? Route? Time? Print it. Give copy to police liaison. When you’re clearly legal, unlawful orders stand out like a baton in a bakery. De-escalation team with vests. Our team wore yellow vests: “PEACE TEAM.” Their job: hug the hotheads (metaphorically), talk down the drunk guy, pull back the kid who wants to throw. They also filmed everything — two phones per team, power banks, livestream. Brain-Optional hates livestream the way vampires hate garlic. Grandmas front, sound truck middle, medics back. Front line sitting if charged. Hands up, palms open. Chant: “We are peaceful — film this.” It’s hard to beat people chanting they’re peaceful while sitting. It looks exactly like what it is. No masks for throwing, no sticks, no bottles. We banned them ourselves. Anyone masked and throwing was isolated — our peace team pointed: “That guy is not with us.” That denies police the excuse of “mixed violent crowd.” It also protects us from infiltrators who love a good smash. Talk to Mario before march. We started meeting the station a day before. “We’ll be 500, route X, end 8pm, our liaison is Ana with red cap, yours?” Most cops relaxed visibly. Only Brain-Optional was disappointed — no war, no story for the bar. Ana (red cap) to line: “Officers, we’ll keep right lane free, kids in middle, we end at 8, okay?” Mario: “Deal. I’ll put two guys at the intersection so buses pass.” Brain-Optional: “...” (kicking pebble, dreaming of riot) Useful lesson: discipline is our shield. Humor is our sword. Cameras are our witnesses. Paper is our revenge. 9. What Commanders Fear More Than Bricks: Cameras, Grandmas, and Paperwork Let me be blunt, human to human: commanders don’t fear your chant. They fear your folder. After Dona Lurdes fell, Ana did three things that night that scared the station more than any brick: uploaded video with time-stamp, took Lurdes to clinic for a report (bruise, shock), and filed a complaint with number, names, badge numbers she’d memorized by flirting with Mario (“for the report, handsome, your badge?” — he laughed and gave it, because good cops aren’t afraid of names). That folder grew: 12 videos, 3 medical reports, 1 cookie receipt, 40 witness contacts. It went to the ombudsman, the press, the councilwoman. The lieutenant who ordered “push” got called to explain. povertyAndFaith: Home Monkey Blog · Data Dossier · Dossier de Dados English Português Politics, Law & Justice · Data Dossier The Poor and the Faithful A serious answer to a question many people carry silently: is it my impression, or is poverty in Muslim countries less harsh and less radical than in Christian countries? The honest answer needs numbers, real examples on both sides, and one distinction that almost every argument about this skips. Poverty Religion & data Welfare Muslim-majority countries Christian-majority countries Bilingual 1. The claim, stated properly The question, as it is usually asked in Portuguese, runs like this: «Será impressão minha ou nos países muçulmanos a pobreza não chega a ser tão dura e tão radical, quanto aos países cristãos?» — is it my impression, or in Muslim countries does poverty not become as hard and as radical as in Christian countries? It deserves a straight answer, because the question underneath it is legitimate even when its framing is not: people notice that the poorest places they hear about in the news are often Christian-majority (Haiti, the favelas of Brazil, the street homeless of Los Angeles) and that the Muslim-majority countries they see in images look organised, hospitable and often rich (Doha, Dubai, Istanbul). Both observations are real. Neither one is evidence. Three clarifications before the data, because they decide everything that follows. An impression measures visibility, not poverty. What you can see is filtered by press freedom, by whether begging is tolerated in public, by where tourists are taken, and by which disasters get cameras. Extreme rural poverty in the Sahel, in Afghanistan or in Bangladesh is far less photogenic than a tent on a Los Angeles pavement. "Muslim countries" and "Christian countries" are not comparable units. There are around fifty Muslim-majority states, several of them among the richest on earth per person and several among the poorest. Christianity is the majority religion in roughly half the planet's countries — Norway, Haiti, the Philippines, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and the United States are all in the same group. Any average across such a group hides more than it shows. Poverty is not a religion and religion is not an income. The measurable drivers of destitution are the ones the World Bank, the UN and national statistical offices keep testing: state capacity, conflict, growth, the distribution of land and oil rents, education, health systems, jobs and social transfers. Religion can shape some of those — through charity institutions, family norms, law — but it is not the variable that does most of the work, and no dataset has ever shown that it is. So this dossier does three things: it gives the numbers for both groups, it takes the part of the question that is defensible and shows exactly what produces it, and it names the part that is not defensible. It is not an attack on the question. It is an attempt to answer it better than it was asked. 2. How poverty is measured, and why that decides the answer Almost every dispute about "which poverty is worse" is really a dispute about the instrument. There are four instruments in common use, and each one is honest about something different. The international poverty line. The World Bank anchors it to the national poverty lines of the poorest countries. In June 2025 it was updated to $3.00 per person per day (2021 prices), replacing the old $2.15 line. It measures whether a household can buy a survival basket of food and essentials. It says nothing about dignity, debt, housing quality or safety. The multidimensional poverty index (MPI). Built by UNDP and OPHI, it counts deprivations in health, education and living standards — nutrition, child mortality, years of schooling, school attendance, cooking fuel, sanitation, water, electricity, housing, assets. It catches the poverty that a market basket misses, and it is the measure in which "poverty is harsh" is most visible. National poverty lines. Each country's own threshold. Useful for trend, useless for comparison: the Philippines' 15.5 per cent in 2023 and Yemen's 74 per cent in 2022 are not measuring the same basket of goods. Relative poverty , used by the OECD (below half the median income of the country). This is the measure that shows poverty in rich countries — the reason Israel can record 21 per cent poor in 2024 and the United States 10.6 per cent in 2024 while Yemen records 74 per cent. The consequence is blunt: a Christian-majority country with a weak welfare state and high inequality will look poor on the relative measure and fine on the absolute one; a Muslim-majority rentier state with oil money and a tiny citizen population will look rich on both while holding hundreds of thousands of migrant workers outside its social contract entirely. If the question uses "poor" to mean "living on very little money" the answer comes from the first two instruments. If it uses "poor" to mean "falling behind the neighbours you can see", it comes from the fourth, and then the comparison is between welfare states. The same two countries can swap places depending on which line you draw. That is not a scandal about the data; it is the reason any honest answer has to name its measure out loud. 3. The numbers, side by side Three global facts frame everything below. In 2026, about 811 million people — one in ten — live on less than $3.00 a day , a rate essentially unchanged since 2019; more than half of the world's extreme poor live in just nine economies ; and by 2030 about 87 per cent are projected to live in Sub-Saharan Africa or in fragile and conflict-affected states. On the multidimensional measure, 1.2 billion people out of 6.3 billion (18.9 per cent) in 108 countries are in acute multidimensional poverty — the first rise since the index began in 2010 — with 616 million of them in Sub-Saharan Africa (51.4 per cent of its population); more than half of all the multidimensionally poor are children, and eight in ten live in rural areas. The table is a selection of real, documented cases, not a ranking. The filter below the caption switches between the groups. Group All Muslim-majority Christian-majority Neither 15 / 15 Poverty, measured — selected countries, with the instrument and the year Country Majority Measure Latest figure Year Yemen Muslim Multidimensional poverty (UNDP) 82.7 % 2024 Yemen Muslim National poverty line (World Bank) 74 % 2022 Afghanistan Muslim Unable to meet basic needs (UNDP) 74 % — three in four 2025 Gaza (Palestine) Muslim Population below the poverty line (UNCTAD) 100 % — 2.3 million 2025 Nigeria Muslim / Christian Multidimensional poverty (NBS) 63 % — 133 million 2022 Indonesia Muslim Health insurance coverage, JKN 280 million — 98 % 2025 Qatar, the UAE Muslim Income per person (World Bank) about $30,000 to $80,000 a year 2023 DR Congo Christian National poverty line (INS / World Bank) 69 % 2024 Ethiopia Christian Poverty rate, rising again (World Bank) 43 % 2025 Ethiopia Christian Multidimensional poverty 72 % 2024 Haiti Christian Poorest country in the Western Hemisphere (World Bank) 1.5 million displaced 2026 Philippines Christian Official poverty incidence (PSA) 15.5 % — 17.5 million 2023 United States Christian Official poverty rate (Census Bureau) 10.6 % — 35.9 million 2024 Israel Jewish Poverty, national insurance report 21 % — 2 million 2024 India Hindu The $3.00 line, over a decade 27.1 % → 5.3 % 2011 → 2023 Read the table twice. In the first four rows a Muslim-majority country shows some of the harshest poverty recorded anywhere on earth: three quarters of Yemen and of Afghanistan, and the entire population of Gaza. In the next rows another Muslim-majority country shows the opposite extreme, and a fifth — Indonesia — has built a health insurer covering 98 per cent of its population. On the Christian side the same spread appears: the Democratic Republic of the Congo at 69 per cent and Ethiopia at 43 per cent against the United States at 10.6 per cent, with Haiti at the bottom of its hemisphere. And the single largest poverty reduction in the table, India's, happened in a Hindu-majority country. 4. The finding: the difference inside each group is bigger than the difference between them Take the two groups as people usually mean them. Inside the Muslim-majority group, income per person runs from roughly a few hundred dollars a year in Afghanistan to above thirty thousand in Saudi Arabia and above eighty thousand in Qatar: a factor of two hundred between two states that share the same majority religion and, in some cases, the same legal tradition. Inside the Christian-majority group the same spread appears: Norway, Denmark and Switzerland at the top of every human-development table, the Democratic Republic of the Congo at 69 per cent below the national poverty line and Haiti the poorest country in its hemisphere. That spread is the whole answer to the original question, and it is not a rhetorical trick. It is what the World Bank's own data show when you stop averaging: poverty is not distributed by creed, it is distributed by geography, conflict and rent. In 2026 more than half of the world's extremely poor live in nine economies — a set that includes Muslim-majority, Hindu-majority and mixed states — and by 2030 about 87 per cent of them are projected to be in Sub-Saharan Africa or in fragile and conflict-affected situations. On the multidimensional measure, the deepest concentration on earth is Sub-Saharan Africa, with 616 million people (51.4 per cent) — a region that is roughly half Muslim and half Christian. Africa does not sort by religion. It sorts by war, by colonial borders, by commodity prices and by the capacity of a state to collect taxes and deliver services. Three consequences follow, and they are worth saying plainly. One Muslim-majority country cannot be compared with one Christian-majority country, and neither can the averages. With roughly fifty Muslim-majority states and about half the world's countries being Christian-majority, the groups contain both the richest societies ever measured and some of the poorest. The comparison people actually make is between subsets. In practice the eye compares the Gulf with Haiti, or Istanbul with a favela in Rio. Those are real photographs, but they are comparing the wealthiest corner of one group with the poorest corner of the other. The strongest correlates of destitution are known and boring: war, state capacity, dependence on a single commodity, tropical disease burden, isolation from markets, education, and whether women are permitted or able to work. The World Bank's 2026 assessment put a number on the last one: raising employment in poor households, including by closing the gender gap, would cut global extreme poverty by roughly a fifth. If the same religion produces both the richest and the poorest states in the file, then religion is not the variable doing the work. Something else is, and that something else is what this dossier is searching for. 5. Where the impression is half right — three real mechanisms There is a defensible version of the question, and it deserves real examples rather than a shrug. Three mechanisms genuinely soften the edge of poverty in specific Muslim-majority countries. None of them is the religion itself, and all three have Christian-majority equivalents or failures. A. Rent shared with citizens The Gulf states built their welfare on hydrocarbons: free or cheap energy and water, subsidised food, guaranteed public-sector jobs, no income tax, generous family allowances, and — after the price reforms — explicit cash compensation. Saudi Arabia's Citizen's Account , introduced with the 2018 round of energy reforms, was designed precisely to keep low- and middle-income households whole after the price rises; Iran did the same thing on a bigger scale in 2010, when it raised energy prices to market levels and paid a monthly transfer to almost every citizen (445,000 rials per person per month at the time), which economists still study as the largest such swap ever attempted. The result is real: some of the least visible poverty on earth, among citizens. The mechanism is the rent, not the faith. The proof is the rest of the class: Nigeria, Iraq, Angola, Libya and Algeria are oil states with mass poverty; Venezuela and Equatorial Guinea are oil states in other religious categories with the same result. Oil money makes a state generous to its own population when the population is small, and it does nothing of the kind when it is large or when the money is captured. B. Obligatory almsgiving and endowed charity as institutions Zakat is the most interesting of the three, because it has no exact Christian equivalent: it is a compulsory levy , commonly 2.5 per cent of qualifying wealth, and in several countries the state collects it. In Pakistan it is deducted at source from bank accounts; in Saudi Arabia, Malaysia and Sudan it is collected by official bodies; Indonesia has a national agency (BAZNAS) that reported around Rp 32.3 trillion collected in 2023 against an estimated national potential several times larger. Global estimates of annual zakat flows range from $200 billion to $1 trillion (a UNDP estimate quoted in the Islamic Development Bank's own materials) to $550–600 billion (a UN-ESCWA compilation). Even the lowest figure dwarfs global humanitarian aid. Historically the same logic ran through the waqf , the charitable endowment: hospitals, schools, fountains, soup kitchens and caravanserais financed by assets locked out of inheritance. Compare the instruments honestly: Christian charity has the tithe, the parish, the religious order and the relief agency — Caritas, the Salvation Army, the food banks — and these are voluntary or congregational, not a levy with state collection. That difference is real. What it produces, however, is not a gentler poverty but a different plumbing of relief. Egypt's Takaful and Karama transfers went from about 1 million households in 2018 to 4.5 million in 2025 ; Pakistan's BISP reaches many millions of households and is the country's largest social assistance programme; Indonesia's JKN health scheme covers 280 million people, about 98 per cent of the population . Those are state programmes funded by taxation and transfers as much as by alms, and they exist alongside zakat rather than instead of it. C. Family absorption, remittances and the taboo on visible begging The third mechanism is the household. In many Muslim-majority societies the informal obligation to feed a cousin, to host a relative, to send money home from the Gulf, is strong and enforceable through honour. Egypt, Pakistan and Bangladesh are among the world's largest recipients of worker remittances; a house in Kerala or a shop in Sylhet may be financed entirely by a brother abroad. Together with the norm that begging is shameful and should be handled privately or through the mosque, this produces something measurable and something optical at the same time. The measurable part is real relief to millions of people. The optical part is the point of this whole dossier: the same mechanism that genuinely softens some poverty also hides it. Poverty absorbed inside a family, a village or a mosque network does not appear on the pavement, so a foreign visitor does not see it. That is what produces the impression in the question, and it is also why the multidimensional index — which counts sanitation, schooling, fuel, nutrition, child mortality — repeatedly finds severe deprivation in countries whose streets look calm. One more equality, to keep the ledger straight: the world's most effective anti-poverty programmes of the last thirty years came mostly out of two traditions — the Nordic welfare state and the Latin American conditional cash transfer. Bolsa Família in Brazil, a Christian-majority country, kept 8.6 million people out of poverty between 2023 and 2024; without the social programmes, Brazil's extreme poverty rate would have been 10.0 per cent instead of 3.5 per cent. Mexico's Progresa-Oportunidades exported the model to dozens of countries. Bangladesh's BRAC exported its own: the Graduation approach, which lifts ultra-poor households out of destitution with assets, training and a stipend, and now runs in dozens of countries of every religion. 6. Where the impression breaks — the same countries, worst cases Now the other half of the same group. If the question were true as stated, the following situations should not exist. They do. Yemen. A Muslim-majority country in which 74 per cent of the population was below the national poverty line in 2022 (World Bank) and 82.7 per cent were multidimensionally poor in 2024 (UNDP). It is hard to find a harsher, more radical poverty on the planet, at any latitude. Afghanistan. Three out of four people unable to meet their basic needs in 2025, according to UNDP's own socioeconomic review — a figure that would have been called unthinkable in 2001. Gaza. UNCTAD's assessment in November 2025 found the economy collapsed by 83 per cent in 2024 and the entire population — 2.3 million people — below the poverty line. A UN report in July 2025 put poverty in Gaza near 100 per cent, up from 64 per cent before the war. The Sahel and the Horn. Niger, Mali, Burkina Faso, Chad and Somalia are Muslim-majority and among the poorest states in the world; the Sahel concentrates jihadist war, drought, displaced populations and state collapse. Somalia is routinely listed by World Bank-based compilations among the ten poorest countries on earth. South Asia. Bangladesh's programmes exist precisely because ultra-poverty there was extreme — people living on less than the cost of a minimum food basket, sleeping hungry, without assets. Pakistan's rural poverty and northern Nigeria's deprivation are of the same severity. The Gulf's own excluded class. This is the sharpest counterexample of all. In 2019 the ILO counted 24.1 million migrant workers in the Arab States , most of them in the Gulf, most of them from Muslim-majority countries themselves — Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal, Indonesia, Egypt, Ethiopia. They build the cities, clean the houses and dig the foundations, they are usually excluded from the welfare, the subsidies, the citizenship and often the labour law, and their status can depend on a single employer under the sponsorship system. A poverty that is real, but kept off the census and off the pavement. The pattern in that list is not religion. It is war and state failure (Yemen, Afghanistan, Gaza, Somalia, Mali), plus the exclusion of non-citizens from a welfare state whose benefits were never designed for them. Both of those mechanisms exist in Christian-majority countries too — in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, in Haiti, in Guatemala, among migrant workers in the United States and in the Gulf of the Christian Atlantic. 7. The Christian-majority side of the same pattern To answer the question fairly, the comparison has to be run in both directions, with the same instruments. The least poverty ever measured is Christian-majority — and it is not charity Norway, Denmark, Finland and Iceland are Lutheran-majority societies with the lowest poverty rates in the historical record, and the mechanism is not religious: it is state capacity. They tax around half of national income, deliver universal services, insure wages, and let the state, not the family or the parish, absorb shocks. Across the OECD, public social spending averaged about 21 per cent of GDP in 2024 , with Austria, Finland and France above 30 per cent. A technical manual for people who want to own their machine: install it, harden it, encrypt it, quiet it. Three operating systems, one discipline — Windows , Linux and FreeBSD — taught in fourteen gated levels with real commands, real failure modes, and a check at the end of each level that you must pass before the next one opens. Scope Host + network + terminal Levels 13 validated · 1 appendix Prereqs Computer literacy only Revision 2026.10 (autumn) §0 Front matter · read this first How to use this manual without lying to yourself Privacy work fails for two reasons: people copy commands they do not understand, and people believe a single tool solves a structural problem. This manual is built against both failure modes. Rule 01 Read, then run Every command is annotated with what it changes and how to undo it. If a line has no explanation, treat it as hostile — including lines in this manual. Rule 02 Verify, don't trust Checksums, signatures, systemctl status , pfctl -sr , packet captures. A setting you did not verify is a setting you do not have. Rule 03 Threat model first Hardening without a model produces anxiety, not privacy. Level 1 exists to stop you from encrypting the wrong disk for the wrong reason. 0.1 The gate mechanism Levels unlock in order. Each level ends with a validation check of four to six questions: multiple choice, multiple answer, and command construction. You need 75 % or better to open the next level. Wrong answers are explained on the spot, and you may retake a check immediately — the point is comprehension, not punishment. Progress (unlocked levels, scores, checklist state, your threat model) is kept in localStorage under tpm.manual.v1 . Nothing leaves the page. If you clear site data, you start over. Printing the page ignores the locks so you can take a dead-tree copy to a machine that has no browser. Accessibility escape hatch The sidebar's Instructor mode unlocks every level for reading while keeping the checks available. Use it if you are auditing the document, teaching from it, or if a gate is blocking legitimate review. The default is strict. 0.2 Notation Conventions used in every level Mark Meaning $ cmd Run as your normal user. # cmd Run with root privileges ( sudo , doas , or a root shell). /dev/nvme0n1 Example device. Yours will differ — always confirm with lsblk or gpart show before writing to a disk. ⚠ irreversible The command destroys data or is hard to roll back. Pause and re-read. Verification The observable evidence that the change actually took effect. Autopsy A pointer to Level 15, where the popular-but-wrong version of the advice is dissected. What this manual is not It is not legal advice, and it is not a guarantee. Privacy is a property of a system plus its operator plus the adversary's budget. Everything here reduces specific risks; nothing here makes you invisible. Claims of invisibility are a sales tactic. 00 Level 00 · Foundation · ~40 min Threat modeling before tooling “Private” is not a checkbox. It is a relationship between what you have, who wants it, and what they are willing to spend. Get this wrong and every later level becomes theater. Prereq: none Reading + lab Gate: 4 questions ◆ Level locked Finish the previous check first This level opens when you have validated the one before it. Go to the prerequisite 0.1 Four words people use interchangeably Precision here saves money and misery later. These are not synonyms, and vendors deliberately blur them. The properties, defined operationally Property Question it answers Typical control Typical failure Confidentiality Can someone read it? Disk encryption, TLS, access control Key stored on the same disk; screen unlocked Integrity Can someone change it? Signatures, Secure Boot, hashes, file integrity monitoring Unsigned updates, writable /boot Availability Can you still use it? Backups, redundant keys, recovery codes Lost LUKS header, forgotten passphrase, dead YubiKey Anonymity Can the action be tied to any identity? Tor, mixnets, cash, compartmentalization Logging in “just once”; unique writing style Pseudonymity Can actions be tied to a consistent identity that is not your legal one? Separate personas, aliases, dedicated browser profiles Personas leak into each other through metadata, payment, timing Unlinkability Can two observations be proven to be the same person? Compartmentalization, fingerprint resistance, traffic padding Reused email, reused avatar, same IP, same hour of day The practical takeaway Encryption gives you confidentiality, not anonymity. Tor gives you a degree of anonymity, not confidentiality of what you type into a website. Backups give you availability and can destroy confidentiality if they are unencrypted. You will almost always be trading one for another. 0.2 The adversary ladder Rank adversaries by capability, not by how scary their name sounds. Each rung below can do everything the rungs above it can do, plus more. Design for the rung you actually face; designing for the top rung with a bottom-rung budget produces paralysis. A1–A5: who is actually looking Rung Adversary Capabilities What actually helps What does not A1 Opportunistic trackers, ad networks, data brokers Cookies, pixels, SDKs, purchased data, probabilistic matching Browser hardening, DNS filtering, aliases, opt-outs VPNs (they see you anyway), “incognito” A2 Platforms (OS vendor, app stores, social networks) Telemetry, account graphs, on-device scanning features, cloud sync Local accounts, telemetry policy, no cloud sync, app permissions Deleting the app but keeping the account A3 Network: ISP, employer, hotel, mobile carrier Flow metadata, DNS, SNI, captive portals, lawful interception Encrypted DNS, HTTPS everywhere, VPN/Tor, MAC randomization, no auto-join HTTPS alone against metadata A4 Targeted: stalker, competitor, ex-partner, fraudster OSINT, phishing, credential stuffing, SIM swap, physical access Hardware keys, unique passwords, number hygiene, FDE, tamper evidence “I have nothing worth stealing” A5 State-level / legal process Subpoenas, compelled keys (jurisdiction-dependent), implants, supply chain, traffic analysis Compartmentalization, minimized data, legal counsel, Tor, air gaps Consumer VPN marketing Autopsy 01 A VPN moves your trust from the ISP to the VPN operator. It does not make you anonymous to the websites you log into, and it does not stop browser fingerprinting. If your adversary is A3, that trade can be worth it. If your adversary is A5 and you are the target of legal process, a VPN with your name on the invoice is a witness, not a shield. Full dissection: Level 15 §15.1 . 0.3 The five questions Write the answers down. A threat model that only exists in your head is a mood. The template below is deliberately small; it is based on the standard “what / who / what if / what then” structure used in security engineering. What am I protecting? Data, identity, location, relationships, availability of a service, reputation. Be concrete: “my tax records and the fact that I am looking for a new job.” From whom? Pick a rung from the ladder. Name at least one realistic actor. “Everyone” is not an actor. What happens if it fails? Embarrassment, money, employment, safety, legal exposure. Impact drives how much friction is justified. How likely is it? Opportunistic dragnet (near-certain) versus targeted intrusion (rare but severe). Product matters more than sum. What am I willing to spend? Money, time, convenience, and the patience of the people who share your life. An unmaintainable setup fails open. Worked example 1 — the developer with a day job Assets: source code, cloud credentials, personal email, home address. Adversary: A1/A2 for marketing data, A4 for credential stuffing and package-supply-chain attacks. Impact: account takeover, doxxing, employer breach. Budget: two evenings, no recurring cost. Resulting controls: full-disk encryption on the laptop, password manager with unique passwords, WebAuthn keys for email and code host, 2FA on cloud accounts, browser compartmentalization, DNS filtering, no personal data in public git commits, and a .gitconfig that does not leak a private address. Worked example 2 — the journalist covering local government Assets: source identities, unpublished drafts, location patterns. Adversary: A3/A4 plus the possibility of A5 through legal orders. Impact: source harm, physical risk. Budget: moderate, ongoing. Resulting controls: Signal with disappearing messages for sources, Tor Browser for sensitive research, an air-gapped or dedicated device for the most sensitive material, encrypted backups with keys held offline, a documented data-retention policy, and a pre-agreed plan for device seizure. Note what is not on the list: a consumer VPN. Worked example 3 — the FreeBSD hobbyist Assets: a home server with family photos and SSH access to a VPS. Adversary: A1 scanning bots and A4 credential stuffing; occasional physical access by guests. Impact: botnet enrollment, data loss. Resulting controls: key-only SSH, pf deny-by-default, jails for exposed services, automated encrypted backups, ZFS snapshots, and a router-level rule that exposes exactly one port. Their threat model does not justify Tor; it justifies patching. 0.4 The baseline every model includes Regardless of rung, some controls have no meaningful downside. Do these before optimizing anything exotic. Universal wins, in order of return on effort # Control Why it is near-universal 1 Patch promptly Nearly all mass compromise uses known vulnerabilities. An unpatched machine with perfect privacy settings is still owned. 2 Full-disk encryption + a screen lock Protects the largest realistic loss: a stolen or repaired device. 3 Password manager + unique credentials + WebAuthn where offered Removes credential reuse, the single biggest account-takeover vector. 4 Encrypted, tested backups Ransomware and disk failure are privacy events too: they expose or destroy data. 5 Separate admin and daily accounts Limits the blast radius of any single compromise. 6 Browser hygiene Most tracking happens in the browser, not the OS. 7 Minimize accounts and data Data you never gave away cannot leak. Deletion is weaker than non-collection. 8 Encrypted DNS with a deliberate resolver Cheap, reversible, removes a rich metadata source from the local network. 9 Turn off cloud sync you do not need Sync turns a local compromise into a total one, and vice versa. 10 Write down your recovery plan Availability is part of privacy. Which property does full-disk encryption actually provide? Confidentiality of the data at rest Anonymity for its owner Availability of the data Unlinkability between accounts Why: FDE protects data at rest: without the key, the contents are unreadable. The assets you are protecting The adversary's capability and motivation The impact if the protection fails The brand of browser you prefer Why: A threat model names assets, adversaries, impact, likelihood and budget. Harden the browser and filter tracking at the DNS and request level Buy a VPN subscription Reinstall the operating system Replace the home router Why: A1 tracking happens mostly in the browser. Current workarounds, in order of reliability: Local-account routes, with honest caveats Method How Caveat OOBE local-account shell Shift + F10 → start ms-cxh:localonly Works on 24H2/25H2 today; Microsoft can remove it at any time. Unattended answer file autounattend.xml on the USB root with a LocalAccounts pass Most robust; requires you to write XML and re-create media. Disconnect + domain join (Pro) Shift+F10 → ipconfig /release , then “Continue with limited setup” Home builds now require connectivity; Pro is more forgiving. Convert after OOBE (Pro) Settings → Accounts → Your info → “Sign in with a local account instead” Home hides this; the MSA and its cloud data still exist until deleted. Both use AES-XTS under the hood, but only BitLocker lets you require a PIN at boot and choose the key protector mix. TPM-only BitLocker is convenient and defeats a thief who pulls the drive; it does not defeat an attacker who can boot your machine and attack the TPM flow, or a cold-boot attack against a suspended laptop. Administrator · enable BitLocker with TPM + PIN manage-bde -status C: Conversion Status: Fully Decrypted Encryption Method: None # 1) Create a recovery password first and store it OFF this machine manage-bde -protectors -add C: -RecoveryPassword Key Protectors Added: Numerical Password ID: {A1B2C3D4-…} manage-bde -protectors -get C: Numerical Password: 123456-234567-… (write this on paper, offline) # 2) Add a TPM+PIN protector, then start encryption manage-bde -protectors -add C: -TPMAndPIN manage-bde -on C: -EncryptionMethod XtsAes256 Encryption started. This may take a while. Verification: manage-bde -status C: must say Fully Encrypted , XtsAes256 , and list both TPM+PIN and Numerical Password protectors. Reboot and confirm you are prompted for the PIN before Windows starts. Key management is the whole game A BitLocker recovery key stored in account.microsoft.com/devices/recoverykey is escrowed. Print it, store it in a safe, and delete the online copy if your threat model includes legal process. Losing every protector means permanent data loss — BitLocker has no back door for you either. Firmware changes break TPM-only boots BIOS updates, Secure Boot key changes and some dock firmware can invalidate the TPM measurements and trigger recovery mode. That is the security model working. Keep the recovery password current and offline; do not “fix” it by deleting protectors. 1.4 First thirty minutes: a defensible default Do these in order on a fresh install. STK aims to change how people understand themselves and interact with their communities, and that kind of mission is never simple. Acknowledging the risks isn’t a sign of weakness—it’s a sign of maturity and responsibility. By understanding what could go wrong, we give ourselves the power to make things go right. ⚠️ Where Failure Could Come From Several challenges could affect the long‑term success of STK: Low user engagement : If too few people participate—uploading videos, voting, forming groups, or rating qualities—the platform loses its purpose. STK depends on community activity. Misunderstanding the platform’s goals : Some users may see STK as a competition or a popularity contest instead of a tool for self‑improvement and social awareness. Lack of trust : If users don’t feel safe sharing videos or receiving feedback, they may hesitate to participate. Technical limitations : Bugs, slow performance, or difficulties with video uploads can discourage new users. Group inactivity : If groups don’t form or don’t solve challenges, one of the most powerful features of STK becomes underused. Negative or unhelpful feedback culture : If users misuse the rating system or comments become discouraging instead of constructive, the platform’s spirit can be damaged. These risks are real, but they are not inevitable. They simply highlight the areas where we must focus our energy. 🌱 How We Reduce the Chances of Failure Success doesn’t happen by accident—it happens through consistent effort from both the platform and its community. Here’s how we can strengthen STK and make it thrive: 🌟 1. Build a Supportive Community Encourage users to give thoughtful, respectful feedback. Remind everyone that the goal is growth, not judgment. A positive culture attracts more people and keeps them active. 📣 2. Spread the Word STK grows when people talk about it. Sharing the platform at school, work, cafés, churches, or among friends helps create a diverse and active community. The more voices, the more meaningful the experience becomes. 🎥 3. Create and Participate Regularly Uploading videos, voting on others’ actions, and rating qualities keeps the platform alive. Even small actions help maintain momentum. 🤝 4. Form and Support Groups Groups are essential for large‑scale challenges. Encouraging organizations, clubs, or community teams to join strengthens the platform’s social impact. 🔧 5. Improve the Platform Continuously Developers and users should work together to identify bugs, suggest improvements, and refine the experience. Every update reduces friction and increases trust. 🛡️ 6. Promote Transparency and Safety Clear rules, respectful communication, and privacy options help users feel secure. When people trust the platform, they participate more freely. 🚀 Failure Is Possible — But So Is Something Much Greater STK can fail if it becomes forgotten, misunderstood, or misused. But it can succeed—beautifully—if people believe in its purpose and participate with honesty and curiosity. The future of STK doesn’t depend on luck. It depends on us: the users, the groups, the creators, and the communities that choose to grow together. If we commit to using STK with intention, kindness, and consistency, the probability of failure becomes small—and the potential for positive change becomes enormous. Join the movement. psicopatia: É difícil, na condição pessoal Existem alguns indicadores do que poderá ser um potencial psicopáta, sendo que dentro da psicopatia, poderá haver um grande número de individuos que não sentem necessidade de cometer crimes, mas há também uma pequeno número que poderá cometer um ou mais crimes, sendo que a maioria desses crimes, terão um desenvolviment minimamente "requintado". O termo "requintado", aqui usado, serve para descrever como os crimes serão produzidos. É extremamente difícil reconhecer um psicopáta via a observação do individuo no seu estado normal e solitário, mas é extremamente fácil na condição de socialização onde o "investigador" cria um ambiente ora de humor ora de choro, o qual irá criar aos presentes, uma qualquer irregularidade expressiva. Caso um dos individuos não demonstre expontaneidade emocional, ora de aceitação ora de negação da expressão que foi declarada para todos publicamente, temos aqui um potencial psicopáta. A psicopatia está associada à falta de emoção e como tal, à falta de capacidade de criar uma relação "normal" em diferentes situações puramente sociais, tendo em conta que o individuo não irá ter variações expressivas. Na confrontação do óbvio, as perguntas podem ajudar a identificar este tipo de pessoas, caso a pessoa não tenha conhecimento sobre a "subjectividade corporal" que é impossível de descrever de forma comum para todos, além das palavras usadas para simplificar esses mecanismo corporais. Por exemplo: Qual é a diferença entre alegria e tristeza? Qual é a diferença entre prazer e dor? Qual é a diferença entre admiração e ódio? Um potencial psicopáta que não sabe identificar essas diferenças, irá responder a todas as perguntas acima descritas da seguinte forma: ( não existe diferença ). Ora, é normal que sem capacidade sensíveis e físicas, de identificar ou experienciar as irregularidades emocionais que cada qual poderá sentir nos diferentes momentos das suas vidas, não seja possível saber a diferença entre dor ou prazer. É por causa desta característica, que um pequeno ou até, grande número de mulheres, sentem-se atraídas por este tipo de pessoas, pois a demonstração de consistencia emocional, indica às mulheres que existe uma espécie de segurança emocional e como tal, segurança para ser capaz de viver em paz, pois a maioria das mulheres são mais emocionais do que a maioria dos homens, por condição natural. Por isso, não é surpreendente que um psicopáta seja apreciado e desejado por várias mulheres, sendo que a maioria dessas mulheres, poderão ser assassinadas pelos seus amantes preferidos. Um evento bem comum, que se repete há mais de 40 séculos de história, nos diferentes países deste mundo, sendo que os homens que demonstram ter irregularidades expressivas e emocionais, raramente têm sorte com as mulheres, pois por ordem do desenvolvimento dos animais, as mulheres têm tendência de escolher os mais fortes, e não os mais sensíveis. Sendo que, caso haja uma irregularidade demasiado intensa do reflexo emotivo, poderemos estar a lidar com um potencial sociopáta, que ao contrário do psicopáta, sente em demasia e por isso, irá sentir necessidade de cometer um crime, como reflexo da "dor" que sentiu após uma qualquer declaração puramente verbal, ou até em alguns casos, por causa de características físicas que outras pessoas apresentam, que lhes cria essa vontade de forma descontrolada. Se contar uma piáda, a maioria dos presentes poderão rir-se, sendo que poderá haver pessoas que não consideram que a piáda tenha piáda, negando rir mas demonstrando-se chateadas pela forma como o humorista brincou com um qualquer assunto. Como houve uma responsa expontanea, (mesmo sendo de negação) é uma demonstração de que não existe o potencial de psicopatia. Num grupo, é fácil identificar potenciais psicopátas, pois a única característica que poderemos considerar "normal", está na tentativa de integrar-se no ambiente que é capaz de percepcionar com um pequeno atraso temporal. Depois de contar uma anedota e a maioria demonstrar graça, o psicopáta poderá começar a rir-se passado alguns segundos, mas esse riso não é genuíno, é sim reproduzido artificialmente para se sentir incluído. Estatísticamente, considera-se que na America Latina, haja um grande número de sociopátas, tal como nos países nordicos europeus, um grande número de psicopátas, principalmente como resultado ora do ambiente, ora das técnicas educativas, usadas culturalmente. Este tipo de resultados devem-se quase sempre, a abusos que cada um dos diferentes individuos, tiveram como experiencia de vida. Este artigo continua aqui .

É isso que este artigo tenta fazer: a origem, o símbolo do Tigre, a mensagem que ele carrega em Lisboa e na Ásia, as divisões que existem hoje, o que cada uma faz, o que funciona e o que desmorona.
